facts.fact: The WHO and ministry assessment of September 2022 states that the Federal Ministry of Health runs the national HMIS on DHIS2 from its own data centre with a cloud-based server, with an HMIS structure connecting district, region, state and federal levels.

The assessment states that strengthening the health information system is entirely dependent on donors, that the Global Fund contracted the University of Oslo to build the HMIS rolled out in 2017, and that this over-reliance fragments the system and weakens ministry leadership (September 2022).

As of September 2022 the assessment counts 641 facilities reporting to DHIS2: 3 national hospitals, 26 regional hospitals, 35 district hospitals, 5 private hospitals, 386 health centres, 140 primary health care units and 46 TB centres, excluding Somaliland.

The assessment states that although DHIS2 allows direct entry, in practice most facilities record on 12 standard paper registries and send monthly summary forms to the district HMIS officer, who enters them into DHIS2; only 30-42% of districts have such an officer (September 2022).

The assessment lists digitalisation of data entry as being piloted at selected health facilities, with no count given, and names digitalising data at facility level as a priority still to be taken to scale (September 2022).

The assessment lists among the weaknesses of the public routine system that there is no electronic medical records system (September 2022); it adds that the private sector uses a variety of health information management software, undescribed.

The assessment states that public facilities record patients on standard paper registries supplied by the ministry, including inpatient and outpatient registers, and that there is no electronic medical records system (September 2022).
With no electronic medical records system in the public sector, the assessment records no primary facility keeping digital patient records (September 2022).

facts.fact: The WHO and ministry assessment of September 2022 states that the Federal Ministry of Health runs the national HMIS on DHIS2 from its own data centre with a cloud-based server, with an HMIS structure connecting district, region, state and federal levels; Somaliland keeps a separate DHIS2 instance.

The assessment states that strengthening the health information system is entirely dependent on donors, lists the Global Fund and UNICEF as the funding source of DHIS2 in its Annex 1, and says the over-reliance weakens government leadership (September 2022).

The assessment lists as weaknesses the absence of a unified health information system strategic plan and the lack of an e-health strategy, and scores a national e-health policy or strategy as not present; its roadmap sets an HIS strategy for 2023 and an e-health strategy for 2024 (September 2022).

As of September 2022 the assessment counts 641 facilities reporting to DHIS2: 3 national hospitals, 26 regional hospitals, 35 district hospitals, 5 private hospitals, 386 health centres, 140 primary health care units and 46 TB centres, excluding Somaliland; it says DHIS2 is used in public facilities across the country and covers only the public sector.

The assessment states that although DHIS2 allows direct entry, in practice most facilities record on 12 standard paper registries and send monthly summary sheets to the district HMIS officer, who enters them into DHIS2; its Annex 1 gives the source data as paper entered at district or regional level, and only 30-42% of districts have such an officer (September 2022).

The assessment lists digitalisation of data entry as being piloted at selected health facilities, with no count given, and names digitalising data at facility level as a priority still to be taken to scale (September 2022).

The assessment lists among the weaknesses of the public routine system that there is no electronic medical records system and that no standardised hospital information management system is in place, public hospitals recording on a mix of paper, Excel and DHIS2; its Annex 1 notes electronic medical records in private clinics and hospitals, undescribed (September 2022).

The assessment states that public facilities record patients on standard paper registries supplied by the ministry, including inpatient and outpatient registers, and its working groups scored a system for collecting patient management data at the point of service as not present (September 2022).

With no electronic medical records system in the public sector, the assessment records no primary facility keeping digital patient records; its roadmap sets designing, piloting and implementing one for 2023 to 2027 (September 2022).

facts.fact: The Ministry of Health's bulletin for July to September 2023 states that the ministry decided to use DHIS2 as the exclusive national HMIS platform for routine health information, run by its HMIS Section, with no other vertical health data collection allowed.

The bulletin states that the ministry's Health Information Section and its partners prepared and finalised a five-year costed Health Information Strategy, and that HSSP III and the Investment Case 2022-2027 set DHIS2 as the single national reporting platform; no date of finalisation is given, so the bulletin's quarter is used.

The ministry reports 579 public health facilities reporting to DHIS2 in July to September 2023, against 532 in the same quarter of 2022, on data sets for health-centre outpatients and hospital outpatients and inpatients, at an aggregate reporting rate of 95.8% (86.8% in Q3 2022); it gives no breakdown by hospital level or facility type, and puts private hospitals' reporting rate at 2%.
The bulletin states that the ministry's HMIS section initiated the pilot of electronic health records, on RAAD EMR, in partnership with SPIDER (July to September 2023).
The bulletin states that the electronic health records pilot is supported by the Government of Sweden through SPIDER (July to September 2023).
